analysis.one_liner: Bars federal contractors and states receiving federal money from sending government contract work offshore.
analysis.headline: The bill to bar offshoring of federal and state government contract work was introduced in February 2004, referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal procurement law to stop companies from performing work on US government contracts from other countries. It would have applied to jobs moved from federal employees to contractors and to federal service contracts generally, allowing exceptions only when the work had to happen overseas or the President decided it was needed for national security. It would also have cut off federal money to any state whose governor did not certify that no federal funds would be spent on work performed abroad. The bill was sent to a Senate committee and never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: US workers holding or seeking jobs on federal and state government service contracts would gain if the bill passed, because their work could not be shipped offshore to foreign workforces. This was a live issue in 2004, when companies were moving call-center, data-processing, and technical support jobs to countries like India. State and local workers competing against offshore contractors for federally funded projects would also benefit once the certification requirement took effect two years after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US federal and state contract workers

how_it_helps.text: It barred contractors from performing federal work offshore unless federal employees had done that work abroad before the job was converted to a contractor.

It prohibited work on federal procurement contracts from being performed outside the United States unless the work had to happen abroad to meet an overseas requirement, with a national-security waiver available from the President.
It required each state's governor to certify before April 1 that no federal grant money would be spent on work performed offshore, with the requirement starting two fiscal years after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Government contractors and offshore service providers would bear the cost, losing the ability to lower prices by performing federal and state work in countries with cheaper labor. Taxpayers and states might face somewhat higher contract costs and new paperwork requirements: states would have to certify annually that no federal funds go to offshore work, and federal agencies would have to police compliance. Consumers of the same offshore services in the private market would see no change, since the bill covered only government work.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have imposed new certification paperwork on all 50 states and conditioned federal money on compliance, which governors and states often resist as an intrusion on state contracting authority.

Barring performance abroad could raise the cost of some government services, since some work is cheaper to perform offshore, and contractors might have met the rules by restructuring work through subcontractors.
The bill exempted work already performed abroad and allowed a broad national-security waiver by the President, limiting how much offshoring it actually stopped.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For federal and state contract work, the gains to US workers were real and the costs to consumers or taxpayers were modest, since the bill covered government contracts and federally funded state contracts rather than private outsourcing generally. The main drawbacks are the compliance burden on states, the risk of contractors avoiding the rules through subcontracting, and possible federal-state friction. The bigger honest objection is scope: it addressed only government work, a slice of the offshoring problem, and it reached the floor only as a small appropriations provision in 2004 rather than through this bill, which never moved.

outcome.mechanism: Dodd introduced the bill in February 2004, the Senate sent it to its Governmental Affairs Committee, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dodd introduced the United States Workers Protection Act of 2004 on February 12, 2004.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs the same day; the bill text notes it was referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
No further action appears in the record: the committee held no markup, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and no vote was ever taken.
The bill's congressional page shows it expired at the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005, having died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government contractors and offshore service providers kept the ability to perform federal and state contract work from abroad, since no restrictions were enacted. Federal and state contract workers who might have gained the jobs got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Government contractors and offshore service providers

for.name: Sen. Christopher J. Dodd
for.role: US Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 12, 2004, to bar offshoring of federal and state government contract work.

for.name: One Republican Senator
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both parties.

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it, held no markup, and never let it reach the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, but with no recorded votes or committee action, no partisan split ever formed.

industries.industry: Government contractors and offshore service providers
industries.note: The bill would have barred these firms from performing US government work from offshore locations, cutting off a fast-growing way to lower the cost of federal and state service contracts. In 2004, moving call-center, IT, and back-office work abroad was a major part of the government services business.

industries.industry: US-based federal and state contract workers
industries.note: Work that would have been sent offshore would have stayed with workers in the United States, protecting jobs in call centers, IT services, and other government contract work. This is labor rather than an industry, but they were the bill's intended beneficiaries.
